## Why This Is Asked

This tests precise bit-twiddling with non-trivial masks and no loops, a common optimization pattern.

## Key Concepts

- Mask construction for adjacent-bit swaps
- Two-shift strategy and one return
- Edge cases: 64-bit boundaries, unsigned masking

## Code Example

```c
uint64_t swapAdjacent64(uint64_t n) {
  const uint64_t E = 0x5555555555555555ULL;
  const uint64_t O = 0xAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAULL;
  return ((n & E) << 1) | ((n & O) >> 1);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you generalize to swap every 3-bit group? 
- What are the performance implications on modern CPUs?

Tests low-level bit manipulation skills without branches, common in performance-critical code. It demonstrates proper masking, shifting, and word size preservation.

- Bit masking with 0x5555 (even positions) and 0xAAAA (odd positions)

```c
uint16_t swapAdjacentBits16(uint16_t x) {

```

- Input: `0b11110000` (240) → Output: `0b11110000` (240)

static inline uint32_t swapRedBlue32(uint32_t color) { uint32_t red = (color & 0x00FF0000) >> 16; uint32_t blue = (color & 0x000000FF) << 16; return (color & 0xFF00FF00) | red | blue; }

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to implement a small, practical bit rotation using only shifts and OR, a common low-level operation in compilers and algorithms.

## Key Concepts

- Bit shifts and masking
- Width awareness and undefined behavior avoidance
- Circular wrap-around without loops

## Code Example

```c
uint32_t rotateLeft32(uint32_t n, unsigned r) {
  unsigned s = r & 31;
  return (n << s) | (n >> (32 - s));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you generalize to 64-bit n?
- What if language semantics define undefined shift amounts; how to guard?
